hullBase
DATA501 project, R package version 0.1.0
Thanya Manivannan

1OVERVIEW

Project objective
  • Address one limitation of the rubberband method, which is that the lower convex hull cannot follow a concave region of the baseline
  • Keep the rubberband method as the primary method and add the detection and correction of concave regions
Package
  • hullBase, version 0.1.0, MIT licence
  • One main function, correct(), which returns a BaselineModel
Spectra hullBase is designed for
  • hullBase corrects the baseline of FTIR spectra recorded as absorbance against wavenumber (cm⁻¹)
  • In absorbance the peaks point upwards, so the rubberband lies underneath the spectrum
  • Spectra recorded as transmittance are not corrected by hullBase and must be converted to absorbance, A = −log10(T), before calling correct()
  • The baseline is a gradually shifting background below the peaks, and the corrected spectrum is y − b
Figure. Simulated FTIR spectrum corrected by hullBase. The hullBase baseline follows the concave baseline when the spectrum is in absorbance and every peak is narrower than peak_width.

2LIMITATION THE PACKAGE ADDRESSES

How the plain rubberband works
  • The rubberband stretches underneath the spectrum and touches the low lying points, called hull points
  • The straight lines between neighbouring hull points are the hull segments
  • At each hull point the hull can only bend upwards
The limitation
  • Where the true baseline bends downwards, a concave region, the hull touches only the two ends of the region
  • The hull segment runs straight underneath the concave region
  • The gap between the segment and the true baseline remains in the corrected spectrum, so peaks on that region are measured too tall
Figure. Example illustrating the limitation of the plain rubberband baseline, computed with lower_hull() on two spectra from simulate_spectrum(). Left, the hull follows the convex baseline. Right, the hull runs straight underneath the concave baseline.
Note
The package hullBase addresses only this limitation, where a hull segment runs straight underneath a concave region of the baseline.

3WHAT THE PACKAGE DOES

Figure. The three steps of the correction and the function that performs each one.
What changes
  • Every hull segment of the plain rubberband is tested
  • A flagged segment is bent locally to follow the concave region
  • Every other segment keeps the plain rubberband line
What is calculated from the data
  • Which segments to bend, from a threshold set from the noise level of the spectrum
  • How strongly to bend, from the estimated height of the concave region
  • peak_width is set by the user

4PACKAGE STRUCTURE AND MAIN FUNCTIONS

4.1PACKAGE NAME

The package name is available. hullBase is not among the 25,422 packages on CRAN, in any letter case.

4.2FILES AND FOLDERS

Figure. Package layout. R code in R/, C++ code in src/, tests in tests/testthat/ and help pages in man/.

4.3THE SIX BUILDING BLOCKS

Main function
  • correct() runs the full correction and returns a BaselineModel
  • lower_hull(), noise_estimate(), detect_concave_segments() and refine_segment() can also be called on their own
S3 class and methods
  • BaselineModel with print(), summary() and plot()
  • correct() is an S3 generic with a default method and a data frame method
C++ functions
  • lower_hull_cpp() builds the hull and erode_cpp() computes the moving minimum, both through Rcpp
Datasets
  • simulate_spectrum() creates spectra with a known true baseline
  • SrE.IR is loaded from its own package
Tests
  • 8 test files, 79 test_that() blocks and 452 expectations
R CMD check
  • 0 errors, 0 warnings and 0 notes
Note
A test block checks one rule, and an expectation is one single check inside it. Some blocks check the same rule on many different spectra, for example 50 random spectra, so one block can contain 50 checks. This is why 79 blocks give 452 expectations.

What a simulated spectrum stores
Every point stores its true baseline, signal and noise. The noise added at 30 dB is 0.0322.
Note
No measured data is stored in hullBase. SrE.IR is loaded from the ChemoSpec package, so its GPL data is not copied into the MIT licensed package.
Limitation
  • One measured dataset with 16 spectra is a small sample
  • Measured spectra have no known true baseline, so accuracy is measured only on simulated spectra
  • The noise estimate and threshold in hullBase assume independent Gaussian noise, and the package was evaluated only on Gaussian peaks with independent Gaussian noise

6.3THE TWO LOOPS INSIDE correct()

  • Loop 2 visits only the flagged segments and bends each one

7CHECKPOINT A: PREPROCESSING THE INPUT SPECTRUM

MAIN FUNCTIONcheck_spectrum()
PURPOSE
check_spectrum() checks the input spectrum and stops invalid input before any baseline correction is done.
IMPLEMENTATION
check_spectrum() is called first by every function that takes a spectrum, sorts the points by wavenumber and checks the spacing against h, the median step.
EVIDENCE
CheckInput triedResult
numeric, same length, 5 or more pointsletters as x, lengths 5 and 4, only 4 pointsstops with its own message for each case
no NA, NaN or Infan NA inside ystops with a message
sort by xx = 3, 1, 2, 5, 4returns sorted data, ord = 2, 3, 1, 5, 4, h = 1
every x appears oncex = 1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 6stops with a message
spacing within 1 percent of hx = 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7warning, correction continues
Valid input passes check_spectrum() and returns the sorted spectrum and h.
Invalid input is stopped by check_spectrum() with its own message for each problem.
Limitation
  • Repeated wavenumbers, unevenly spaced wavenumbers and transmittance spectra must be prepared by the user before calling correct().

8CHECKPOINT B: CONSTRUCTING THE LOWER CONVEX HULL

MAIN FUNCTIONlower_hull()
PURPOSE
lower_hull() computes the plain rubberband baseline, which is the starting baseline of hullBase.
IMPLEMENTATION
lower_hull() passes the sorted points to lower_hull_cpp(), which finds the hull points with Andrew’s monotone chain algorithm and the 2D cross product, in one scan from left to right.
EVIDENCE
163 expectations in test-lower_hull.R pass, including the comparison with grDevices::chull() on 50 random spectra.
Figure. Plain rubberband baseline computed with lower_hull() on a simulated spectrum. The hull segments run straight underneath the concave true baseline.
lower_hull() on y = 5, 2, 3, 2, 5 removes the point lying above the line between its neighbours and returns 5, 2, 2, 2, 5.
lower_hull_cpp() and lower_hull_r() give identical hull points on one spectrum of 500 random points, and the baseline never goes above the data.

9CHECKPOINT C: ESTIMATING NOISE AND DETECTING CONCAVE REGIONS

MAIN FUNCTIONdetect_concave_segments()
PURPOSE
detect_concave_segments() flags only the hull segments that hide a concave region, so that only those segments are bent in Checkpoint D.
IMPLEMENTATION
Function called inside detect_concave_segments()What it does
check_spectrum()checks and sorts the input spectrum, and returns the step h
noise_estimate()estimates the noise level of the spectrum from its second differences, when the user does not give a noise value
lower_hull_cpp()finds the hull points, and gives the hull segments to be checked
erode_cpp()applies a moving minimum as wide as peak_width to the residual above each hull segment, so the peaks are removed and the concave region remains

detect_concave_segments() flags a segment when its largest eroded value exceeds the threshold calculated from the noise level, and returns a table of the decision for every hull segment.

noise_estimate() on the simulated spectrum gives 0.0335 against the true noise standard deviation of 0.0322.
Figure. The residual above the hull segment from 13 to 1396 and its moving minimum from erode_cpp(). The moving minimum removes the peaks, and the eroded residual of the concave region exceeds the threshold.
detect_concave_segments() with peak_width = 300 returns one row for each of the five hull segments, and only the segment from 13 to 1396 is flagged, with a largest eroded value of 0.936 against the threshold of 0.255.
Limitation
  • detect_concave_segments() cannot tell a peak wider than peak_width apart from a concave region, so the user must set peak_width at least as wide as the widest peak.
  • detect_concave_segments() does not flag a concave region lower than the threshold, so under such a region the plain rubberband line remains.
  • detect_concave_segments() calculates the threshold from noise_estimate(), which assumes the noise of neighbouring points is independent, so on spectra with correlated noise, such as SrE.IR, the threshold may be set too high or too low.

10CHECKPOINT D: BENDING A FLAGGED SEGMENT

MAIN FUNCTIONbend_segment()

called by correct() for each flagged segment, and available to the user through refine_segment()

PURPOSE
bend_segment() replaces the straight hull line under a flagged segment with a baseline that follows the concave region, while every other segment keeps the plain rubberband line.
IMPLEMENTATION
Function called inside bend_segment()What it does
erode_cpp()removes the peaks from the residual above the flagged segment, so the height of the concave region can be estimated
lower_hull_cpp()takes the lower convex hull of the spectrum after the bending curve is added
bend_segment()calls itself on any part of the concave region that still exceeds the threshold, up to 3 levels

bend_segment() adds a bending curve with strength twice the estimated height, takes the hull, then subtracts the curve.

Figure. Left, the flagged segment from 13 to 1396 with the bending curve added, and the hull of the bent spectrum. Right, the hullBase baseline after the bending curve is subtracted, with the true baseline.
refine_segment() on the flagged segment lowers the RMSE against the true baseline from 0.742 for the plain rubberband baseline to 0.054, and correct() gives the same baseline on this segment.
Limitation
  • bend_segment() gives a baseline made of straight lines joined at corners, not a smooth curve.
  • bend_segment() uses bend_factor = 2, which was tested only on the half sine concave baseline of the simulated spectra.

11CHECKPOINT E: RETURNING AND INSPECTING A BaselineModel

MAIN FUNCTIONcorrect()
PURPOSE
correct() runs every checkpoint in order and returns one BaselineModel object that holds the result and the information needed to inspect it.
IMPLEMENTATION
Function called inside correct()What it does
check_spectrum()checks and sorts the input spectrum
noise_estimate()estimates the noise level when the user does not give one
lower_hull_cpp()gives the plain rubberband baseline, which is stored for comparison
detect_concave_segments()flags the hull segments that hide a concave region
bend_segment()bends each flagged segment

correct() is an S3 generic with a default method for x and y, and a method for a data frame. Its result has print(), summary() and plot() methods.

correct() returns an object of class BaselineModel with 10 fields, and print() shows that one of five hull segments was refined.
summary() reports the noise estimate, the threshold, the refined segment from 13 to 1396 and how far the baseline was lifted above the plain rubberband baseline.
Figure. Left, plot() shows the spectrum with the plain rubberband baseline and the hullBase baseline, and shades the refined segment. Right, plot() with which = "corrected" shows the corrected spectrum.
The data frame method and the default method of correct() give the same baseline.
Limitation
  • correct() has no default value for peak_width, so the result depends on a value the user must choose, and a peak_width smaller than the widest peak leaves that peak treated as part of the concave region.
  • correct() does not record how many bending levels were used, so when the limit of 3 levels is reached, the user is not told that part of the concave region may still remain above the baseline.
  • correct() corrects one spectrum per call, so the user must write a loop to correct a set of spectra, and the same peak_width is then applied to every spectrum unless the user changes it.

12RESULTS ON EVERY DATASET

12.1SIMULATED SPECTRA

Mean RMSE against the true baseline over 20 spectra for each baseline shape and noise level, for the plain rubberband baseline and for hullBase.
On the simulated FTIR spectrum, correct() refines one of three hull segments, and the RMSE against the true baseline falls from 0.216 to 0.010.
Figure. Corrected simulated FTIR spectrum from 400 to 4000 cm⁻¹.
RESULT
The RMSE for concave and mixed baselines falls at every noise level. For flat, linear and convex baselines it is unchanged, because no segment is flagged.
CONDITIONS

Conditions of the simulated spectra under which this result was obtained

  • the noise is independent and Gaussian, so noise_estimate() gives the noise standard deviation and the threshold is at the intended level
  • every peak is Gaussian and narrower than peak_width = 300, so the moving minimum removes every peak
  • the spectrum is in absorbance and evenly spaced, with each wavenumber only once
  • the concave baseline has a half sine profile of height 1, which is above the threshold
Limitation
  • simulate_spectrum() creates spectra that meet every condition above, so the result does not show how hullBase performs when one of these conditions does not hold.
  • The result was obtained with peak_width = 300 and bend_factor = 2 only, so the effect of other values on the error was not measured.
  • The hullBase error on concave baselines rises from 0.056 at 30 dB to 0.223 at 20 dB, so the improvement is smaller on noisier spectra.

12.2MEASURED SPECTRA

Figure. SrE.IR sample 1 corrected with peak_width = 300 (top) and peak_width = 800 (bottom). The baseline under the band group from 500 to 1500 cm⁻¹ is lifted at peak_width = 300 and follows the plain rubberband line at peak_width = 800.

13LIMITATIONS OF THE PACKAGE

LimitationWhy it is a problem
peak_width is chosen by the userwhen peak_width is smaller than the widest peak, the peak survives the moving minimum, is taken as part of the concave region and is removed from the corrected spectrum
detection depends on the noise levelthe threshold rises with the noise, so on noisy spectra a concave region is not flagged and stays under the plain rubberband line
noise is assumed independent and Gaussianmeasured spectra such as SrE.IR do not meet this assumption, so the threshold may not be at the intended level
the baseline is made of straight linesthe hullBase baseline has corners at the hull points and is not a smooth curve
the input must be preparedrepeated wavenumbers, uneven spacing and transmittance spectra must be corrected by the user before calling correct()
Figure. With peak_width = 50 on the simulated FTIR spectrum, the peaks are wider than the moving minimum window, so every hull segment is flagged and the hullBase baseline rises into the peaks.
The peak at 3300 cm⁻¹ with a true height of 0.25 keeps a height of 0.026 with peak_width = 50 and 0.264 with peak_width = 300. On a simulated concave spectrum at 10 dB, correct() refines none of the seven hull segments.

13.1FUTURE IMPLEMENTATION

Not yet evaluatedFuture implementation
peak shapes other than Gaussian, such as Lorentzian or asymmetric peaksadd these peak shapes to simulate_spectrum() and repeat the evaluation on 300 simulated spectra
noise whose size changes across the spectrumestimate the noise level separately for each hull segment, and test detection on simulated spectra with changing noise
measured spectra with a known reference baselineevaluate the package on measured spectra whose reference baseline is known, so the baseline error can be calculated
comparison with other baseline methodscompare the package with other baseline correction methods, such as a penalised least squares baseline, on the same simulated and measured spectra

14CONCLUSION

What the package does
  • hullBase addresses one limitation of the plain rubberband baseline, a hull segment running straight underneath a concave region.
  • correct() keeps the plain rubberband line on every hull segment and bends only the flagged segments.
What the package is
  • hullBase is a refinement of the rubberband method, not a new baseline correction method.
  • The lower convex hull is computed in the standard way, and the refinement is the local bending of flagged segments, with the bending strength calculated from the data.
